facts.fact_text: At around 2.20 p.m. on 29 June 2006, the applicants began a demonstration outside the Tbilisi Court of Appeal.
The purpose of the applicants' demonstration on 29 June 2006 was to express their support for Mr Shalva Ramishvili and Mr Davit Kokhreidze.
According to the applicants, the court bailiffs restrained the applicants by force allegedly without prior warning or explanation.
The applicants were taken into the court-house after being restrained by the bailiffs.
The applicants were locked in the bailiffs' duty room of the court-house.
According to the applicants' written statements of 4 and 5 July 2006, no record of the applicants' arrest was drawn up on the spot.
According to the applicants' written statements of 4 and 5 July 2006, the applicants were not shown any arrest record.
According to the applicants' written statements of 4 and 5 July 2006, the applicants were not asked to sign any arrest record.
The bailiffs reassured the applicants that they were not formally under arrest, that it was a simple misunderstanding, and that they would soon be released.
The case file contained five separate records of arrest, one for each applicant.
The arrest records indicated the name of the drafting bailiff for each applicant.
The arrest records indicated the name, date of birth, address, and full serial number of the identification card of each of the applicants.
The arrest records stated that the applicants had been arrested at around 2.20 p.m. on 29 June 2006.
The arrest records stated that the applicants had been arrested on the basis of section 76(3) § 1 (f) of the Courts of Common Jurisdiction Act of 13 June 1997.

The arrest records stated that the offenders had "breached public order" in the form of "contempt of court, insults, disregard of the bailiffs' lawful orders to stop the wrongdoing, resistance to the bailiffs, attempts to influence the court by actions and verbal expressions, impeding the administration of justice, and so on".
All arrest records contained an entry in the drafting bailiff's handwriting indicating that the applicants had "refused to sign this record or to receive a copy thereof".
According to the applicants, the records of their arrest were drafted and added to the file concerning their case ex post factum.
The applicants were confined in the duty room of the court-house for some three hours in complete unawareness of the reasons for their detention.
After being confined in the duty room, the applicants were transferred by the police to an Interior Ministry remand centre.
The case file contains an excerpt from the relevant prison log showing that the fourth applicant entered the Interior Ministry remand centre at 5.45 p.m. on 29 June 2006.
The arrest records stated that the applicants had been arrested on the basis of section 76(3) § 1 (f) of the Courts of Common Jurisdiction Act of 13 June 1997.

Section 76(3) § 1 (f) of the Courts of Common Jurisdiction Act of 13 June 1997 required bailiffs to prevent offences from being committed inside the court-house, identify offenders and, if necessary, arrest them for the purpose of handing them over to the police, and draft a written record on such arrests.

Section 76(3) § 2 (a) of the Courts of Common Jurisdiction Act of 13 June 1997 gave bailiffs the right to resort to physical force, to "special equipment" and even to firearms in the exercise of their duties.

Section 76(4) § 1 of the Courts of Common Jurisdiction Act of 13 June 1997 specified that the right to resort to physical force, special equipment and firearms could be exercised only if other less severe measures of constraint had been shown to be ineffective.
Section 76(4) § 4 of the Courts of Common Jurisdiction Act of 13 June 1997 specified that bailiffs were obliged to issue a verbal warning to the persons concerned prior to resorting to force.
Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, on the basis of which the applicants were sanctioned by the decision of 29 June 2006, was titled "Liability for breach of public order in court".

Article 208 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provided that the President of the court shall ensure the maintenance of public order in the court, whilst the presiding judge shall be responsible for maintaining order during the hearing of cases.

Article 208 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provided that a party to the proceedings, or any other person who has either breached public order during a hearing, or disregarded the presiding judge's ruling or is in contempt of court, shall be fined and/or expelled from the courtroom.

Article 208 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provided that if the person expelled from the courtroom continues to breach such an order, the detention envisaged by Article 208 may be imposed upon him or her.

Article 208 § 6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provided that if manifest and gross contempt of court has been shown, the judge presiding over the hearing may issue a decision to detain the offender for up to thirty days, and such a decision shall be enforced immediately.

Article 208 § 6(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure provided that in the event of a breach of public order or contempt committed inside the court building, the President of the court shall be entitled to apply the measures envisaged by Article 208 against the offender.

Article 208 § 7 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provided that decisions of the presiding judge and of the President of the court under Article 208 shall be delivered by on-the-spot deliberations and without an oral hearing, and no appeal shall lie against them.
Subsequent to the Constitutional Court judgments of 15 December 2006, Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was significantly revised on 29 December 2006.

The newly added paragraph 8 of Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure explicitly gave court bailiffs the power to arrest a person who had either "breached public order in the court, was in contempt, or had obstructed the normal functioning of the court".

Under the revised Article 208 § 8 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, bailiffs were obliged to draw up a record of such arrests and to bring the offenders before the President of the relevant court within twenty-four hours.
Under the revised Article 208 § 8 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the President had a further twenty-four hours to issue a decision on whether to punish the offender.

Paragraphs 10 and 11 of the amended Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure stated that proceedings concerning the imposition of detention on an offender should always be adversarial and conducted at an oral hearing at which the offender would be given an opportunity to defend him or herself.

Under the amended Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, should the President decide to detain the offender, the latter was entitled to lodge an appeal against that decision with the higher court within the next forty-eight hours.
Court bailiffs were not among the authorities empowered to effectuate an administrative arrest under Article 246 of the Code on Administrative Offences.
Pursuant to Article 247 of the Code on Administrative Offences, administrative arrest must not exceed three hours, unless specific statutes provided for longer terms "in cases of exceptional need".

Articles 252, 263 and 264 of the Code on Administrative Offences contained procedural and substantive rules on the conduct of administrative proceedings, similar to those normally applicable to criminal proceedings in court.
Under Articles 252, 263 and 264 of the Code on Administrative Offences, a person charged with an administrative offence had the right to examine the case materials.
Under Articles 252, 263 and 264 of the Code on Administrative Offences, a person charged with an administrative offence had the right to submit arguments, evidence and requests.

Under Articles 252, 263 and 264 of the Code on Administrative Offences, a person charged with an administrative offence had the right to benefit from legal assistance during the examination of the case.

Under Articles 252, 263 and 264 of the Code on Administrative Offences, a person charged with an administrative offence had the right to plead in his or her native language or to be assisted by an interpreter.
Under Articles 252, 263 and 264 of the Code on Administrative Offences, a person charged with an administrative offence had the right to appeal against procedural rulings.
Under Articles 252, 263 and 264 of the Code on Administrative Offences, an administrative case was always to be examined in the presence of the charged person during an oral hearing.
Under Articles 252, 263 and 264 of the Code on Administrative Offences, in absentia proceedings could take place only if the charged person had been duly summoned but had failed to appear.
Pursuant to Article 271 § 2 of the Code on Administrative Offences, no appeal lay, as a general rule, against a court decision convicting a person of an administrative offence and imposing a penalty.

Pursuant to Article 279 of the Code on Administrative Offences, a final decision could be quashed by means of an extraordinary review, at the request of a prosecutor or by the President of the superior court.

Article 271 § 2 of the Code on Administrative Offences provided: "The city (district) court's decision to impose an administrative penalty is final and not subject to an appeal in administrative proceedings, except for those cases where a law holds otherwise."
The arrest records stated that the applicants had been arrested on the basis of section 76(3) § 1 (f) of the Courts of Common Jurisdiction Act of 13 June 1997.

The arrest records stated that the offenders had "breached public order" in the form of "contempt of court, insults, disregard of the bailiffs' lawful orders to stop the wrongdoing, resistance to the bailiffs, attempts to influence the court by actions and verbal expressions, impeding the administration of justice, and so on".

The President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, Mrs E.T., concluded in the decision of 29 June 2006 that the applicants had "breached public order, shown manifest and gross contempt towards the court and endangered the administration of justice".
The operative part of the decision of 29 June 2006 indicated that no appeal lay against it.
The operative part of the decision of 29 June 2006 indicated that the applicants were to serve their sentence in remand centre no. 2 of the Ministry of the Interior.

All arrest records contained an entry in the drafting bailiff's handwriting indicating that the applicants had "refused to sign this record or to receive a copy thereof".
According to the applicants, the records of their arrest were drafted and added to the file concerning their case ex post factum.
The applicants were confined in the duty room of the court-house for some three hours in complete unawareness of the reasons for their detention.
After being confined in the duty room, the applicants were transferred by the police to an Interior Ministry remand centre.
The case file contains an excerpt from the relevant prison log showing that the fourth applicant entered the Interior Ministry remand centre at 5.45 p.m. on 29 June 2006.
The case file contained explanatory memos from three court bailiffs who had participated in the applicants' arrest.
The explanatory memos from the three court bailiffs were half-page handwritten documents containing similar phrases.
The explanatory memos from the three court bailiffs were addressed to the Chief of the Bailiff Service of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal.
According to the bailiffs' explanatory memos, the applicants, "standing near the public entrance of the court at around 2.20 p.m.", had started "demanding the release of political prisoners".
According to the bailiffs' explanatory memos, the applicants had been "insulting the court by their expressions and actions".
One of the bailiffs stated in his memo that the applicants' actions had amounted to an encroachment upon the court's independence and impartiality.
Another bailiff stated in his memo that the wrongdoers had been trying to influence the court.
All three bailiffs stated in their memos that, prior to resorting to the measure of arrest, they had requested the applicants to stop the disturbance.

When the applicants were transferred to the Interior Ministry remand centre, they learnt that they had been detained on the basis of a decision of 29 June 2006 issued by the President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal.
The decision of 29 June 2006 was a one-page document issued by the President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, Mrs E.T.
The President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, Mrs E.T., sat privately and without holding an oral hearing when issuing the decision of 29 June 2006.
The President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, Mrs E.T., decided to detain the applicants for thirty days on the basis of the bailiffs' written submissions alone.
The detention of the applicants was ordered under Article 208 § 6(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The decision of 29 June 2006 noted the bailiffs' version of the incident, namely that the applicants, "who were inside the court building, in its central entrance, were breaching public order, obstructing the normal functioning of the court and seeking to influence the court with respect to proceedings in a particular case".
The decision of 29 June 2006 noted that despite the bailiffs' request that they stop the disturbance, the applicants persisted with their conduct in the form of "verbal expressions and actions".

The President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, Mrs E.T., concluded in the decision of 29 June 2006 that the applicants had "breached public order, shown manifest and gross contempt towards the court and endangered the administration of justice".
The operative part of the decision of 29 June 2006 indicated that no appeal lay against it.
The operative part of the decision of 29 June 2006 indicated that the applicants were to serve their sentence in remand centre no. 2 of the Ministry of the Interior.
The operative part of the decision of 29 June 2006 indicated that the Tbilisi police department was responsible for its execution.
On 21 July 2006, the applicants requested the Supreme Court of Georgia to examine their complaint against the decision of 29 June 2006 under Article 279 of the Code on Administrative Offences.

The applicants' request to the Supreme Court of Georgia on 21 July 2006 referred to the suspension of the operation of Article 208 § 7 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by the Constitutional Court's decision of 20 July 2006.
The applicants argued before the Supreme Court of Georgia that their detention was an administrative penalty.

The applicants complained before the Supreme Court of Georgia that the President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal had committed a manifest miscarriage of justice by punishing them under Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provision clearly envisaged liability only for acts committed inside court buildings.
The applicants submitted a video recording of their demonstration to the Supreme Court of Georgia to show that it had taken place in the yard of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal.

The applicants argued before the Supreme Court of Georgia that Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure could not be considered a foreseeable and therefore legitimate basis for their conviction and detention.

The applicants complained before the Supreme Court of Georgia that the President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal had violated the principles of a fair trial by delivering her decision entirely on the basis of the one-sided account provided by the bailiffs.

The applicants complained before the Supreme Court of Georgia that the President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal had chosen the severest sanction of those available under Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
On 26 July 2006, Supreme Court judge Mr Z.M. examined the applicants' complaint of 21 July 2006 in absentia.
Supreme Court judge Mr Z.M. dismissed the applicants' complaint of 21 July 2006.
The date of the examination of the applicants' complaint on 26 July 2006 was not communicated to the applicants in advance.

In the decision of 26 July 2006, Judge Z.M. first noted that the suspension of Article 208 § 7 of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not automatically entitle the applicants to lodge an appeal against their detention.
Judge Z.M. acknowledged in the decision of 26 July 2006 that the applicants' detention was, by its nature, an administrative penalty.
Judge Z.M. ruled in the decision of 26 July 2006 that the complaint of 21 July 2006 against the penalty could be examined under Article 279 of the Code on Administrative Offences.
Judge Z.M. criticised the applicants in the decision of 26 July 2006 for abusing their right to freedom of expression.

Judge Z.M. found in the decision of 26 July 2006 that it was established from the case materials that the applicants had truly exhibited "manifest and gross contempt" towards the Tbilisi Court of Appeal by committing those acts "inside the court building, namely in its central entrance hall".

Judge Z.M. stated in the decision of 26 July 2006 that the aim of Article 208 § 6(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was to protect public order not only inside court-houses but also outside them, in adjacent premises.

Judge Z.M. stated in the decision of 26 July 2006 that the President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal had no other choice but to sanction the applicants under Article 208 § 6(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, since what was at stake was "not the judge's own interests but the authority of the court and the proper administration of justice".

In reply to the complaint that the President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal had made her decision entirely on the basis of one-sided submissions, Judge Z.M. stated in the decision of 26 July 2006 that all the evidence — the records of the applicants' arrest and the explanatory notes — had been drafted and submitted by the bailiffs for consideration by the President in accordance with a procedure envisaged by law.
Judge Z.M. stated in the decision of 26 July 2006 that the thirty days' detention had been an appropriate punishment, given the gravity of the acts committed.
The period of the applicants' detention expired and they were released on 28 July 2006.
